q: What is trunk-based development and why does it suit CI/CD?
p: Developers merge small changes to one main branch at least daily, using short-lived branches and feature flags. It keeps integration continuous and avoids long-lived branch merge pain.
tip: Say that flags, not branches, hide unfinished work.
a: Trunk-based development means everyone integrates into a single main branch very frequently, ideally at least daily, using short-lived branches that live hours rather than weeks. It suits CI/CD because continuous integration only works if changes are actually integrated continuously. Long-lived feature branches hide conflicts and create big, risky merges, and they make the pipeline test something that never resembles production. With trunk-based work, unfinished functionality is hidden behind feature flags so main is always releasable. It requires strong automated tests, fast pipelines and small pull requests with quick reviews. Compared with Gitflow, it removes release branches and cherry-pick chaos, though some teams keep short release branches for hotfixes. The benefits are smaller diffs, easier reviews, faster feedback and more frequent deployment. The trade-off is that the team needs discipline and good test coverage, otherwise broken changes reach main more often.
f: How do feature flags fit in?
When would you still use release branches?

q: What are the DORA metrics and how do they relate to CI/CD?
p: Deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service. Together they measure delivery speed and stability.
tip: Emphasise that speed and stability are measured together.
a: DORA metrics are four measures of software delivery performance: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service. The first two describe throughput and the last two describe stability. CI/CD directly influences them. A fast, reliable pipeline shortens lead time from commit to production and enables more frequent deployments. Automated tests, progressive delivery and quick rollback lower the change failure rate and speed up recovery. I would measure them from real data, such as pipeline events and incident records, not from estimates, and look at trends per team instead of ranking people. The research finding is that high performers are good at both speed and stability, so they are not a trade-off. I use the metrics to find bottlenecks, for example long review waits or slow test stages, and I avoid turning them into targets that people could game.
f: How would you collect these metrics?
Why avoid using them as targets?

q: What is the difference between a build artifact and a deployment manifest, and why version both?
p: The artifact is the built binary or image; the manifest says how and where to run it. Versioning both gives reproducible, auditable releases.
tip: Mention that rollbacks need both to be recoverable.
a: A build artifact is the output of the build, such as a container image, a JAR or a binary, identified by an immutable version or digest. A deployment manifest describes how to run it: Kubernetes YAML, a Helm chart with values, or Terraform that defines the runtime. I version both because a release is the combination of the two. If I only version the artifact, I cannot reproduce configuration, replica counts, resource limits or environment settings from last week. If I only version the manifest, it may point at a mutable tag that now refers to different code. Storing manifests in Git gives history, review and easy rollback, and referencing artifacts by digest makes the deployment deterministic. Many teams keep manifests in a separate repository from application code so that configuration changes can be reviewed and promoted without rebuilding the artifact.
f: Why separate config from code repositories?

q: What is a monorepo versus polyrepo pipeline strategy, and how does CI handle each?
p: A monorepo holds many services; CI must detect which changed. Polyrepo has one pipeline per repo but harder cross-repo changes.
tip: Talk about path filters and build caching.
a: In a monorepo, many services and libraries live in one repository. The CI challenge is avoiding building and testing everything on every change. I use path filters or a build tool with a dependency graph, such as Bazel, Nx or Pants, to calculate affected targets and cache results remotely. The advantages are atomic cross-service changes, shared tooling and easy refactoring. In a polyrepo setup, each service has its own repository and pipeline, which gives clear ownership and simple pipelines, but cross-repository changes need coordination, version bumps and compatibility testing. For a monorepo I would also make sure code ownership files, permissions and pipeline times scale, since a single slow pipeline blocks everyone. The right choice depends on team size, coupling between services and tooling maturity, and I would not choose a monorepo without investing in incremental builds.
f: How do you find affected services?

q: What are the stages of a typical modern CI pipeline in order, and why that order?
p: Lint and unit tests first, then build, scan, integration tests, publish artifact. Cheap fast checks come first to fail early.
tip: Explain fail-fast and cost ordering.
a: I order stages from cheapest and fastest to most expensive, so failures are reported early and compute is not wasted. First come static checks: formatting, linting and type checks, plus secret scanning. Next, unit tests, which are fast and need no infrastructure. Then the build of the artifact, followed by security scanning of dependencies and the image. After that, integration tests against ephemeral dependencies, and finally publishing the immutable artifact to a registry, tagged with the commit SHA. Deployment pipelines then promote that same artifact through environments. Some stages can run in parallel, such as linting and unit tests, to reduce wall-clock time. The principle is fail fast: developers should learn about a typo in a minute, not after a thirty-minute end-to-end suite. I also make sure every stage is deterministic and that the pipeline definition lives in version control.
f: Which stages can run in parallel?

q: What is a build agent or runner, and how do you choose between hosted and self-hosted?
p: A runner executes pipeline jobs. Hosted is simple and clean; self-hosted gives control, private network access and cost savings at scale.
tip: Cover isolation, ephemeral runners and secrets.
a: A runner or build agent is the machine or container that executes pipeline jobs. Hosted runners are managed by the provider, start clean for each job and need no maintenance, which is ideal for small teams and public code. Self-hosted runners give control over hardware, such as GPUs or large memory, access to private networks and internal services, and often lower cost at high volume. The risks are security and upkeep. A long-lived self-hosted runner can retain state or secrets from previous jobs and can be attacked through untrusted pull requests. I prefer ephemeral runners that are created per job, for example on Kubernetes or autoscaling groups, with minimal permissions and no access to production credentials unless the job needs them. I would also never run untrusted fork code on runners with privileged network access, and I monitor queue time to scale capacity.
f: How do you secure runners for forked pull requests?

q: What is semantic versioning and how do you automate releases from commits?
p: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH conveys compatibility. Conventional commit messages let tools calculate the next version and changelog automatically.
cmds: git commit -m 'feat: add retry to client'
tip: Mention breaking change markers.
a: Semantic versioning uses MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, where a patch is a backwards-compatible fix, a minor adds backwards-compatible functionality, and a major introduces breaking changes. It communicates risk to consumers. To automate releases I use conventional commit messages, such as feat, fix and a breaking change footer, and a tool like semantic-release or release-please that reads commits since the last tag, calculates the next version, generates a changelog, creates a tag and publishes the artifact. This removes manual version decisions and keeps history consistent. It works best for libraries and APIs. For internal services deployed continuously, many teams version by commit SHA or build number instead, since consumers do not need compatibility signals. The pipeline should only publish from the main branch, require passing checks, and protect the release credentials. I review the setup regularly so it keeps matching how the team really works. I would also measure the effect, so the change is justified by data.
f: How is a breaking change signalled?

q: How do you restrict permissions of the GITHUB_TOKEN in a workflow?
p: Set permissions at the workflow or job level to the minimum scopes and default to read-only.
tip: Least privilege per job.
a: Every workflow run receives a token that can act on the repository, and by default its scope can be broader than needed. I set a top-level permissions block to the minimum, usually contents read, and then grant extra scopes only in the jobs that need them, for example pull-requests write for a commenting job or id-token write for cloud authentication with OpenID Connect. I also set the organisation or repository default to read-only so a workflow that forgets the block is still safe. This limits the damage if a malicious dependency or a compromised action runs in the job, since the token cannot push code or change releases. Combined with pinning third-party actions to commit SHAs and protecting environments with required reviewers, it forms a solid baseline. I review permissions in code review like any other access control change.

q: How do you authenticate a workflow to AWS, Azure or GCP without long-lived secrets?
p: Use OpenID Connect federation: the workflow gets a short-lived token the cloud trusts based on repository, branch and environment claims.
tip: Scope the trust policy to branch or environment.
a: Instead of storing long-lived access keys as repository secrets, I use OpenID Connect federation. The workflow requests a signed identity token from the CI provider, containing claims such as repository, branch, environment and workflow. In the cloud, I create an identity provider trust and a role or workload identity that accepts tokens only when those claims match, for example the main branch of one repository and a production environment. The workflow exchanges the token for short-lived credentials that expire in about an hour. This removes secret rotation and leakage risk, and gives a clear audit trail. The common mistake is a trust policy that is too broad, such as any repository in the organisation, so I always constrain subject claims. I also separate roles per environment so a pull request build cannot deploy to production.
f: What claims should the trust policy check?

q: Why pin third-party actions to a commit SHA, and how do you keep them updated?
p: Tags can be moved; a SHA is immutable. Use an update bot to propose reviewed bumps.
tip: Supply chain risk.
a: A tag or branch reference in a workflow can be moved by the action's maintainer, or by an attacker who compromises their account, so a previously safe step can start running malicious code in my pipeline with access to secrets. Pinning to a full commit SHA makes the reference immutable. The downside is maintenance, since SHAs are unreadable and updates are manual. I solve that with a dependency update bot configured for workflows, which opens pull requests that bump the SHA and show the release notes and diff, so a human reviews each change. I add a comment with the version tag for readability. For critical workflows I also prefer actions maintained by the platform or by my organisation, fork important third-party actions into an internal repository, and restrict the allowed actions list at the organisation level.

q: How do you design environment protection and approvals for production deployments?
p: Use environments with required reviewers, wait timers, branch restrictions and environment-scoped secrets.
tip: Gate on environment, not on person.
a: I model each deployment target as an environment, such as staging and production, and attach protection rules. For production I require reviewers from a specific team, restrict deployments to the main branch or protected tags, and optionally add a wait timer. Secrets and variables are scoped to the environment so a job only sees production credentials after approval. This gives a clear audit trail of who approved what and when. I keep the deploy job separate from the build job, so the same artifact built and tested earlier is promoted, not rebuilt. To avoid approval fatigue, I limit manual gates to production and risky changes, and automate checks like smoke tests and health verification after deployment. For emergencies there should be a documented break-glass path with extra logging, so urgent fixes do not push people to bypass the system.
f: How do you handle emergency deploys?

q: How do concurrency groups prevent overlapping deployments?
p: A concurrency key cancels or queues runs sharing the same group so two deploys do not race.
tip: Cancel for CI, queue for deploy.
a: Concurrency groups let me declare that only one run in a given group can execute at a time. For pull request validation I set the group to the branch and enable cancel in progress, so a new push cancels the outdated run and saves compute. For deployments I use a group per environment and set cancel in progress to false, so runs queue in order and a deployment is never killed halfway, which could leave the system in a partial state. This prevents two pipelines applying infrastructure or migrations at the same time, which can corrupt state or cause race conditions. Combined with state locking in the infrastructure tool, it provides defence in depth. One caveat is that pending runs in a group may be replaced by a newer one, so for strict ordering I design deploys to be idempotent and always deploy the latest commit.
f: When should you cancel in-progress runs?

q: How do you build and publish a container image securely with provenance in a workflow?
p: Build with a pinned builder, sign the image, generate an SBOM and attach provenance attestations.
tip: Sign the digest, not the tag.
a: I build the image using a pinned builder in a clean runner, tag it with the commit SHA and push it, then work with the digest. I enable build provenance and generate a software bill of materials so consumers can see how and from what the image was built. Next I scan the image for vulnerabilities and fail on critical findings with a documented exception process. Then I sign the image digest with a tool like Cosign, preferably keyless using the workflow's identity, so the signature proves it came from my pipeline. In the cluster, an admission policy verifies the signature and refuses unsigned images. The key idea is signing the digest, not a mutable tag. This chain gives traceability from running container back to commit and workflow, which helps with audits and incident response.
f: Why sign digests instead of tags?

q: How do you reduce cost and time of workflows that run on every pull request?
p: Use path filters, caching, concurrency cancel, smaller matrices and skip drafts.
tip: Measure before optimising.
a: I start by measuring which jobs consume the most minutes, then apply targeted fixes. Path filters skip workflows when only documentation changes. Concurrency groups with cancel in progress stop outdated runs after a new push. Dependency and build caches reduce repeated downloads, and I key them on lock file hashes. I trim the test matrix on pull requests to the most important combinations and run the full matrix on main or nightly. Large jobs are split and parallelised, and slow tests are sharded. I use the smallest runner that meets the need and skip expensive jobs for draft pull requests, with a label to opt in. I also set timeouts so stuck jobs do not burn minutes. Finally, I review the bill monthly and track pipeline duration as a metric so regressions are noticed.
f: How do you key a cache?
What should run only on main?

q: What is the danger of pull_request_target and how do you handle workflows for forks?
p: It runs with secrets in the base repository context; checking out untrusted fork code there can leak secrets.
cmds: # avoid checkout of PR head under pull_request_target
tip: Never run untrusted code with secrets.
a: The pull_request event from a fork runs with a read-only token and no secrets, which is safe but limited. The pull_request_target event runs in the context of the base repository with secrets and a write token available. If a workflow using it checks out and executes code from the fork, an attacker can submit a pull request that exfiltrates secrets or pushes changes. My rule is never to run untrusted code in a privileged context. For tasks like labelling or commenting I use pull_request_target without checking out fork code. For building and testing forks I use the plain pull_request event, and if secrets are needed I use a two-stage design: an unprivileged workflow produces artifacts, and a separate privileged workflow consumes them as data only. I also require approval before workflows run for first-time contributors.
f: Why require approval for new contributors?

q: How do you use substitutions and variables in Cloud Build safely?
p: Built-in substitutions like $SHORT_SHA and user-defined ones starting with an underscore let one config serve many environments.
tip: User substitutions must start with underscore.
a: Cloud Build supports built-in substitutions such as project ID, commit SHA, short SHA, branch and tag, and user-defined substitutions that must start with an underscore. I use them so a single configuration file serves multiple environments, for example an environment name and region passed from the trigger, instead of copying files. Values can be set in the trigger definition or on the command line. For security, I never pass secrets as substitutions, because they appear in logs and build metadata. Secrets come from Secret Manager through the available secrets section, which injects them as environment variables only for the steps that request them. In shell steps I need to escape the dollar sign so Cloud Build does not try to substitute shell variables. I also validate substitution values in an early step to fail fast on typos.
f: How do you escape shell variables?

q: How do you run Cloud Build in a private pool and why?
p: Private pools run builds in a VPC-connected, customer-owned environment, allowing access to private resources and custom machine sizes.
tip: Use for private repos and databases.
a: The default Cloud Build workers run in a Google-managed network with public internet access. A private pool is a dedicated worker pool connected to my VPC through private peering, so builds can reach internal resources such as private Git servers, artifact repositories, databases for integration tests or on-premises systems over VPN. It also allows choosing machine types and disk sizes and can disable public IPs, which satisfies strict network policy and data exfiltration controls. The trade-offs are cost, since pools are billed for the workers' use, and extra setup of peering and firewall rules. I use private pools when a build needs private connectivity or compliance requires controlled egress. For ordinary public builds, the default pool is simpler and cheaper. I also combine private pools with VPC Service Controls to limit data movement.

q: How do you speed up Docker builds in Cloud Build using caching?
p: Use Kaniko or BuildKit cache, pull the previous image as cache-from, and order Dockerfile layers by change frequency.
tip: Cache is lost between ephemeral workers.
a: Cloud Build workers are ephemeral, so Docker layer cache does not persist between builds by default. I restore cache in a few ways. One is pulling the previous image and using cache-from, so unchanged layers are reused. Another is using Kaniko with a remote cache repository in Artifact Registry, which stores layers explicitly, or BuildKit with registry cache export. Equally important is Dockerfile ordering: copy dependency manifests and install dependencies first, then copy source code, so the expensive layer is invalidated only when dependencies change. I also use multi-stage builds and a small base image, add a dockerignore file to avoid cache busting from irrelevant files, and pin base image versions. These changes typically reduce build time from minutes to under a minute for incremental changes. The aim is a pipeline people trust enough to ship from on a Friday afternoon. I would also measure the effect, so the change is justified by data.
f: Why is cache lost on ephemeral workers?

q: How do you deploy to Cloud Run from Cloud Build with a gradual rollout?
p: Deploy a new revision with no traffic, test it using a tag URL, then shift traffic in stages and roll back by re-pointing traffic.
cmds: gcloud run services update-traffic app --to-tags canary=10
tip: Revisions are immutable.
a: Cloud Run creates an immutable revision on every deploy, which makes progressive delivery straightforward. In the pipeline I deploy the new image with no traffic and a tag, which gives the revision its own URL for smoke tests. If the checks pass, I shift a small percentage of traffic to it, say ten percent, watch error rate and latency for a defined period, then increase to fifty and a hundred percent. Rollback is just pointing traffic back to the previous revision, which takes seconds and needs no rebuild. I keep the previous revisions available and set the pipeline to automate the checks, using monitoring queries to decide whether to promote or revert. For configuration changes, I include them in the revision so the entire release is atomic, and I make database migrations backwards compatible so both revisions can run together.
f: How do you test the new revision before traffic?

q: How do you control who can trigger builds and what the build can access in Cloud Build?
p: Use a dedicated user-managed service account with least privilege per trigger, and restrict trigger configuration with IAM.
tip: Avoid the default broad build account.
a: By default, builds run as a service account that historically had broad permissions. I create dedicated user-managed service accounts per pipeline with only the roles needed, for example permission to push to one Artifact Registry repository and deploy one Cloud Run service. Triggers are configured with that service account, so a build for a test project cannot touch production. I restrict who can edit triggers and submit manual builds through IAM, because someone who can change a trigger can effectively run code as its service account. For pull requests from contributors, I use comment-based approval so builds do not run automatically with privileged access. Logs go to a controlled bucket, and audit logs record trigger changes. I periodically review service account roles and remove unused ones, and I separate build and deploy accounts for sensitive environments.
f: Why use a custom service account?
How do you handle pull request builds?

q: How do you implement build provenance and attestations on Google Cloud?
p: Cloud Build generates SLSA provenance; Binary Authorization verifies attestations before deployment.
tip: Verify at admission, not just generate.
a: Cloud Build can generate signed provenance for built container images, describing the source repository, commit, builder and build steps, aligned with SLSA levels. It is stored with the image metadata in Artifact Registry. By itself, provenance is only evidence. The value comes from verification. With Binary Authorization on GKE or Cloud Run, I define a policy that requires attestations from trusted attestors, such as one proving the image was built by my official pipeline from the main branch and another proving it passed vulnerability scanning. Deployments of images without valid attestations are blocked. This protects against someone pushing an image built on a laptop or from a compromised source. I also use the break-glass mode with logging for emergencies, and I store the policy in version control so changes are reviewed. I document the decision so new engineers understand why it is built this way. I would also measure the effect, so the change is justified by data.

q: How do you handle drift and self-healing in ArgoCD?
p: Automated sync with selfHeal reverts manual cluster changes to match Git; prune removes resources deleted from Git.
cmds:
syncPolicy:
  automated:
    prune: true
    selfHeal: true
tip: Self-heal can fight emergency changes.
a: Drift occurs when the live cluster differs from what Git declares, for example someone edits a deployment with kubectl. ArgoCD continuously compares them and marks the application out of sync. With automated sync and self-heal enabled, ArgoCD reverts the manual change back to the Git state, and with prune enabled it deletes resources removed from Git. This enforces Git as the single source of truth and helps with audit and security. The trade-off is that during an incident, an engineer's emergency patch will be reverted, so the process must be to commit the fix, or temporarily disable auto-sync on that application with a clear note. Some fields are legitimately changed by controllers, such as replica counts managed by an autoscaler, so I configure ignore differences for those to avoid constant out-of-sync noise.
f: How do you do emergency changes?

q: What are sync waves and hooks in ArgoCD and when do you use them?
p: Waves order resource creation within a sync; hooks run jobs at phases like PreSync and PostSync.
tip: Use for migrations and CRD ordering.
a: By default ArgoCD applies resources in a sensible kind order, but sometimes I need explicit ordering. Sync waves are annotations with an integer: resources in lower waves are applied and must become healthy before higher waves begin. I use them to create namespaces and custom resource definitions before the resources that depend on them. Hooks are resources, usually jobs, that run at specific phases: PreSync before the main sync, Sync, PostSync after success, and SyncFail on failure. A typical use is running a database migration job in PreSync and a smoke test in PostSync. Hooks can be cleaned up automatically with delete policies. I keep hooks idempotent and short, because failing hooks block the sync, and I avoid overusing them since complex orchestration inside a sync is hard to debug. I review the setup regularly so it keeps matching how the team really works. I would also measure the effect, so the change is justified by data.
f: What is a PreSync hook used for?
What happens when a hook fails?

q: How do you structure repositories and environments for ArgoCD: Kustomize overlays or Helm values?
p: A base plus per-environment overlays or values files; promote by changing the image tag or revision per environment.
tip: Directory per environment beats branch per environment.
a: I prefer a directory-per-environment layout on a single branch, rather than a branch per environment, because branches drift and merges become confusing. With Kustomize there is a base containing common manifests and overlays for dev, staging and production that patch replicas, resources and image tags. With Helm there is one chart and a values file per environment. ArgoCD applications point at each environment path. Promotion becomes a pull request that changes the image tag or chart version in the next environment's directory, which gives review, approval and history. Application code and configuration often live in separate repositories so that a config change does not require a rebuild and access can be controlled differently. I keep environment differences small and explicit, and use ApplicationSets to generate applications from the directory structure. The aim is a pipeline people trust enough to ship from on a Friday afternoon. I would also measure the effect, so the change is justified by data.

q: How do you secure ArgoCD itself: RBAC, projects and SSO?
p: Use AppProjects to restrict repos, clusters and namespaces; SSO with group-based RBAC; disable the default admin.
tip: Projects are the multi-tenant boundary.
a: ArgoCD has broad power since it can create resources in clusters, so securing it matters. I configure SSO with the corporate identity provider and map groups to roles, and I disable the built-in admin account after bootstrap. AppProjects define what a team may deploy: allowed source repositories, destination clusters and namespaces, and which cluster-scoped resources are permitted. This stops one team from deploying into another team's namespace or creating cluster roles. RBAC policies grant read, sync or override permissions per project. I restrict who can modify projects and who can sync production. Secrets for repository access use least-privilege deploy keys, and the ArgoCD API is not exposed publicly without authentication. I also enable audit logging and keep ArgoCD upgraded, because it is a high-value target. I document the decision so new engineers understand why it is built this way. I would also measure the effect, so the change is justified by data.

q: How does Argo Rollouts enable canary and blue-green deployments?
p: A Rollout resource replaces Deployment, shifting traffic by steps and analysing metrics to promote or abort automatically.
cmds: kubectl argo rollouts get rollout app --watch
tip: Analysis makes it automatic.
a: Argo Rollouts is a controller that extends Kubernetes with a Rollout resource that replaces the Deployment. For a canary, I define steps such as set weight ten percent, pause, analyse, then fifty percent, and so on, and it uses an ingress controller or service mesh to split traffic. For blue-green, it brings up the new version alongside the old, lets me test the preview service, then switches the active service. The key feature is analysis: AnalysisTemplates query metrics from Prometheus or similar, such as error rate and latency, and the rollout automatically promotes if they stay healthy or aborts and rolls back if they breach thresholds. This turns release verification from manual watching into policy. It works well with GitOps, since the Rollout manifest is stored in Git and ArgoCD syncs it.
f: When is blue-green better than canary?

q: How do you manage multi-cluster deployments and cluster registration in ArgoCD?
p: Register clusters as secrets, use ApplicationSets with cluster generators, and keep a hub-and-spoke or per-cluster instance model.
tip: Hub-and-spoke vs per-cluster instance.
a: ArgoCD can deploy to many clusters. In a hub-and-spoke model, one central ArgoCD instance holds credentials for each target cluster, registered as secrets with a service account token. ApplicationSet cluster generators then create an application per cluster, optionally filtered by labels such as environment or region. The advantage is central visibility and a single control plane. The disadvantage is a larger blast radius and a network and credential dependency on the hub. The alternative is an ArgoCD instance in each cluster, which isolates failures and avoids storing remote credentials, but is more to operate. I choose based on scale and security: highly regulated environments often prefer per-cluster instances, while platform teams managing many similar clusters use a hub. In either case, I use projects to limit what each team can deploy to each cluster.
f: What is the blast radius of a hub?

q: How do you roll back with ArgoCD and why is git revert preferred?
p: Revert the commit in Git so history and cluster agree; UI rollback is temporary when auto-sync is on.
tip: Git is the source of truth.
a: In a GitOps model, Git declares the desired state, so the proper rollback is to revert the offending commit and push it. ArgoCD detects the new commit and syncs the cluster back, leaving a clear audit trail and keeping Git and the cluster consistent. ArgoCD also offers an application rollback to a previous synced revision from its history, which is fast in an emergency, but if auto-sync is enabled it is not allowed or will be overwritten by the next sync, because Git still declares the newer state. So I use the CLI rollback only after disabling auto-sync, and I follow up with a Git revert. For schema changes, rollback also needs backwards-compatible migrations, because reverting the application does not revert the database. Progressive delivery and fast health checks reduce how often rollback is needed.
f: Why does UI rollback conflict with auto-sync?

q: What is the test pyramid and how does it shape pipeline design?
p: Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few end-to-end tests; the pipeline runs cheap tests first.
tip: Inverted pyramids make slow, flaky pipelines.
a: The test pyramid says a healthy suite has many small, fast unit tests at the base, a moderate number of integration tests that check components working together, and a small number of end-to-end tests through the whole system at the top. Unit tests are quick and precise; end-to-end tests are slow, brittle and hard to debug. In the pipeline I run unit tests on every commit, integration tests with ephemeral dependencies on pull requests, and a small set of critical end-to-end smoke tests after deployment to a test environment. An inverted pyramid, with mostly end-to-end tests, leads to pipelines that take an hour and fail randomly, which erodes trust. I also consider contract tests between services as a faster alternative to full end-to-end tests. The goal is confidence per minute of pipeline time.
f: What is the cost of too many e2e tests?

q: How do you test infrastructure as code in a pipeline?
p: Validate syntax, lint, policy-check the plan, and run integration tests in a temporary environment.
cmds: terraform plan -out tfplan && conftest test tfplan.json
tip: Plan is the unit test of IaC.
a: I layer the checks. First static: formatting, validation and linting to catch syntax and provider mistakes. Second, security and policy scanning of the code and the generated plan with tools like Checkov or Open Policy Agent, enforcing rules such as no public storage and mandatory encryption and tags. Third, a plan on every pull request, posted as a comment so reviewers see the exact changes. Fourth, for modules, integration tests that create real resources in a sandbox account, assert behaviour and tear everything down, using a framework like Terratest or the native test command. Apply only runs from main after approval, using the saved plan. I also add cost estimation to the review. Not everything can be mocked, so a small number of real deployments in an isolated account gives the most reliable confidence.
f: What do you check in a plan?
How do you clean up test resources?

q: How do you handle test data and ephemeral environments for integration tests?
p: Use containers or per-PR namespaces with seeded, disposable data and automatic teardown.
cmds: kubectl create ns pr-123 && helm install app ./chart -n pr-123
tip: Never use shared mutable test databases.
a: Shared test databases create flaky tests because runs interfere and data drifts. I prefer disposable environments created per pipeline run: service containers or Testcontainers for dependencies like databases and queues, or a per-pull-request namespace in Kubernetes that deploys the application with its dependencies and is destroyed when the pull request closes. Test data is created by the tests themselves or seeded from versioned fixtures, and never copied from production unless it has been anonymised. Each test should set up and clean up its own state, with unique identifiers so parallel runs do not collide. For heavy dependencies I use lightweight fakes or contract-verified stubs. I add time-to-live labels and a cleanup job so abandoned environments do not accumulate cost. This makes tests repeatable, parallelisable and independent of each other. I review the setup regularly so it keeps matching how the team really works. I would also measure the effect, so the change is justified by data.
f: How do you stop environment sprawl?

q: How do you quarantine and manage flaky tests without hiding real failures?
p: Detect by rerun statistics, move to a quarantine suite with an owner and deadline, and track the flake rate.
tip: Retries hide, quarantine tracks.
a: A flaky test fails intermittently without a code change and destroys trust in the pipeline. I first measure: track pass and fail history per test so flakes are identified by data. Blind automatic retries mask the problem, so I limit them and report any test that needed a retry. A confirmed flaky test moves to a quarantine suite that still runs and reports but does not block merges, with a ticket, an owner and a deadline, otherwise quarantine becomes a graveyard. Meanwhile I look for root causes: shared state, time dependence, ordering, race conditions, network calls and resource limits, and fix them, for example by using fake clocks and unique test data. I publish the flake rate as a metric, and set a team target. The principle is that a red build must mean something.

q: What is mutation testing or coverage gating, and are coverage thresholds useful?
p: Coverage shows what code ran, not whether tests assert behaviour. Mutation testing checks whether tests catch injected bugs.
tip: Use coverage as a floor, not a goal.
a: Code coverage measures which lines executed during tests, but it says nothing about whether the tests verify correct behaviour. A test with no assertions can give high coverage. I use a coverage threshold as a floor and a ratchet, so it cannot decrease, and I apply a stricter requirement to changed lines through diff coverage, which is more meaningful for pull requests. To check test quality, mutation testing introduces small bugs, like flipping a condition, and checks whether tests fail. Surviving mutants show weak tests. It is slow, so I run it on critical modules or nightly, not on every commit. I avoid making coverage a team target to be maximised, since it encourages gaming. Better indicators include escaped defects, and whether tests fail when behaviour changes. The aim is a pipeline people trust enough to ship from on a Friday afternoon. I would also measure the effect, so the change is justified by data.

q: How do you scan for secrets in repositories and block them in CI?
p: Use pre-commit and CI secret scanners, block on detection, rotate any leaked secret and scan history.
tip: A leaked secret must be rotated, not just deleted.
a: I use secret scanning at two points. A pre-commit hook catches secrets on the developer's machine before they enter history, and a CI job scans each pull request and fails if it finds a credential, with a baseline file for known false positives. The platform's push protection can also reject pushes containing known token formats. The most important rule is that removing a secret from the latest commit is not enough: it stays in history and may already have been copied, so the response is to revoke and rotate the credential immediately, then clean history if needed and review access logs for misuse. Prevention matters more than detection, so I steer teams to workload identity and a secrets manager so there are fewer long-lived secrets to leak. I also scan container images and build logs.
f: What reduces the number of secrets?

q: What is an SBOM and how do you generate and use it in a pipeline?
p: A software bill of materials lists components and versions in an artifact, enabling vulnerability lookup and licence checks.
tip: Store it with the artifact.
a: An SBOM is an inventory of the components inside a build, including libraries, versions and licences, in a standard format like SPDX or CycloneDX. I generate it during the build with a tool such as Syft, attach it to the image in the registry as an attestation, and store it alongside the release. Its value shows when a new vulnerability is announced: instead of searching every repository, I can query SBOMs to see which deployed artifacts contain the affected component, and who owns them. In the pipeline I can also scan the SBOM against vulnerability databases, enforce licence policies and compare it to the previous release to detect unexpected new dependencies. Some customers and regulators now require SBOMs. The caveat is that an SBOM is only useful if it is accurate and kept up to date for each release.
f: How does it help when a new CVE is published?

q: How do you apply SAST, DAST and dependency scanning without drowning developers in noise?
p: Tune rules, fail only on high severity new findings, show results in pull requests and track exceptions with expiry.
tip: Fail on new, not old.
a: Each tool covers different risks: static analysis examines source for insecure patterns, dependency scanning finds known vulnerable libraries, and dynamic testing probes a running application. To avoid alert fatigue, I start in report-only mode, tune rules to remove noise, and then enforce gradually. I fail the build only on high or critical findings that are new in the pull request, and treat the existing backlog separately with a remediation plan and deadlines. Results appear as comments or annotations in the pull request, where developers already work, with clear fix guidance. Exceptions require a justification, an owner and an expiry date. I also prioritise by exploitability and reachability, not just severity score. Dynamic scans run against a staging deployment on a schedule, because they are slower. Finally I track metrics like mean time to remediate.
f: What does fail on new findings mean?

q: How do you secure the CI/CD pipeline itself against supply chain attacks?
p: Pin dependencies and actions, least-privilege tokens, isolated ephemeral runners, signed artifacts and protected branches.
tip: Treat the pipeline as production.
a: The pipeline holds credentials and builds what runs in production, so it is a prime target. I apply several layers. Source: protected branches, required reviews, signed commits for sensitive repositories. Dependencies: lock files, hash verification, a private proxy registry, scanning, and pinned versions for build tools and actions. Execution: ephemeral, isolated runners, short-lived credentials from workload identity, least-privilege tokens per job, and no secrets exposed to untrusted pull request code. Output: reproducible builds where possible, signed artifacts with provenance, and admission control that only accepts artifacts from the official pipeline. I also restrict who can edit pipeline definitions, since changing a pipeline is equivalent to running code with its permissions, and I log and alert on unusual changes. Regular reviews against frameworks like SLSA help prioritise improvements. I document the decision so new engineers understand why it is built this way. I would also measure the effect, so the change is justified by data.

q: How do you enforce policy as code for Kubernetes manifests in the pipeline?
p: Validate manifests with OPA/Conftest or Kyverno CLI in CI and enforce the same rules at admission in the cluster.
tip: Shift left, enforce at the gate.
a: Policy as code expresses rules, such as no privileged containers, resource limits required, no latest tags and approved registries only, in a machine-checkable language. In the pipeline, I run a tool like Conftest with Open Policy Agent policies, or the Kyverno CLI, against rendered manifests so developers get fast feedback in the pull request. The same policies are enforced in the cluster by an admission controller, because pipeline checks can be bypassed by direct kubectl access. I begin in audit mode to measure violations, fix common ones, then switch to enforce. Policies live in a version-controlled repository with tests, and exceptions are explicit and time-limited. This keeps standards consistent without relying on manual review, and gives auditors clear evidence of controls. I review the setup regularly so it keeps matching how the team really works. I would also measure the effect, so the change is justified by data.
f: Why enforce at admission as well?
How do you roll out policies safely?

q: How do you manage the approvals and separation of duties required by compliance in CI/CD?
p: Automate evidence, require peer review and protected branches, and separate who writes from who approves production.
cmds: # branch protection: require 1 approval, status checks, linear history
tip: Pipelines can generate audit evidence.
a: Compliance frameworks usually ask for change control, peer review, separation of duties and evidence. In a modern pipeline I satisfy these through automation rather than paperwork. Branch protection requires pull request approval from someone other than the author and passing checks. Deployments to production run through a controlled pipeline with environment approvals by a defined group, and the pipeline records who approved, what was deployed and the test results, creating an audit trail automatically. Developers do not have standing production access; the pipeline's identity does the deployment. Emergency changes follow a documented break-glass process with after-the-fact review. I store pipeline logs and approvals for the retention period. This approach shows auditors a consistent, enforced process, and it is usually faster than manual change advisory boards. The aim is a pipeline people trust enough to ship from on a Friday afternoon. I would also measure the effect, so the change is justified by data.

q: How do you implement blue-green deployment in a pipeline and what are the risks?
p: Deploy to the idle environment, test, switch traffic, keep the old one for rollback; database compatibility is the main risk.
tip: Schema changes must be backwards compatible.
a: Blue-green keeps two identical environments. Blue serves live traffic while I deploy the new version to green, run smoke and integration tests against it, and then switch the router, load balancer or service selector to green. If problems appear, switching back is nearly instant. The benefits are near-zero downtime and fast rollback. The risks are cost, since you run two environments at least briefly, and state. Database changes must be backwards compatible so both versions can work with the same schema, which means using expand and contract migrations. Long-lived connections, sessions and caches also need thought. Also, an all-at-once switch exposes every user to a defect at the same time, so for higher-risk changes I prefer a canary, which limits the blast radius. I keep the blue environment until the new version has proven stable.

q: How do you handle configuration and secrets differences across environments without rebuilding?
p: Build once, inject environment configuration at deploy time from config maps, parameter stores and secret managers.
tip: Same artifact, different config.
a: The same immutable artifact should run in every environment, which means environment-specific values cannot be baked into it. I follow the twelve-factor approach: configuration comes from the environment at runtime. Non-sensitive settings are supplied by Helm values, Kustomize overlays or config maps stored in Git per environment. Secrets come from a secret manager and are injected at deploy or runtime, using an external secrets operator, a CSI driver or workload identity, never committed to Git in plain text. I keep the set of configuration keys identical across environments and validate it in the pipeline, so missing settings fail early. Feature flags handle behavioural differences. This ensures that what was tested in staging is exactly what runs in production, apart from explicit configuration, which makes bugs reproducible and rollbacks safe. I document the decision so new engineers understand why it is built this way. I would also measure the effect, so the change is justified by data.
f: How are secrets injected at runtime?

q: How do you design pipelines for a microservice that depends on shared libraries?
p: Version and publish libraries, use dependency updates automatically, and run compatibility or contract tests downstream.
tip: Avoid lockstep releases.
a: Shared libraries create coupling, so I treat them like products with semantic versions, changelogs and their own pipelines that test and publish to an internal registry. Services pin specific versions and an update bot opens pull requests when a new version appears, so each service upgrades through its own pipeline with its own tests. For critical libraries I run downstream compatibility checks that build a sample of dependent services against the new version before releasing. Contract tests help when the shared element is an API or schema. I avoid forcing lockstep releases of all services, which defeats independent deployability. Deprecation policy matters: announce, support two versions for a window, then remove. If changes happen very frequently across many services, that may be a sign the code belongs in a monorepo or inside a service instead of a shared library.

q: How do you implement automated rollback based on metrics after a deployment?
p: Define SLO-based health checks, observe a bake period, and automatically revert if error rate or latency breach thresholds.
tip: Choose a few strong signals.
a: Automated rollback needs clear definitions of healthy. I choose a small set of strong signals that reflect user experience, such as error rate, latency percentile and saturation, and compare the new version with the baseline over a bake period of several minutes after traffic shifts. The pipeline or a rollout controller queries the monitoring system and decides: promote if healthy, abort and revert if thresholds are breached. Kubernetes readiness probes and rollout status handle basic failures, while progressive delivery tools handle metric analysis. I avoid hair-trigger thresholds that cause rollbacks on noise by requiring sustained breaches and a minimum request volume. Rollbacks must be tested regularly, and database migrations must be compatible. The system should notify the team with the metrics that triggered it, so the failed release is investigated and not simply retried.
f: How do you avoid false rollbacks?

q: What is a deployment freeze or change window, and how do you handle it in modern CI/CD?
p: A period when production changes are restricted. Automate enforcement and keep an emergency path.
cmds: # pipeline rule: block prod deploys if calendar freeze=true unless label=hotfix
tip: Frequent small releases reduce the need for freezes.
a: A deployment freeze restricts production changes during risky periods such as major sales events or holidays. In a modern pipeline I implement it as an enforced rule instead of a convention, for example a check that blocks production deployment jobs when a freeze flag or calendar entry is active, with an override requiring approval and a reason. Hotfixes for security or outages go through an emergency path with extra review and logging. I would also challenge the underlying need: teams that deploy small changes frequently with good rollback tend to have less risk per change, so long freezes can actually increase risk by batching changes. During a freeze I keep merging to main and deploying to non-production, so the backlog is not a large release when the freeze ends. Communication of freeze dates is part of the process.

q: How do you build a pipeline for database schema changes with zero downtime?
p: Use versioned migrations with expand and contract, run them as a controlled step, and keep changes backwards compatible.
tip: Never couple a destructive change to the app release.
a: For zero downtime, the application and schema must work together across versions. I use the expand and contract pattern. In the expand phase I add new columns or tables in a backwards-compatible way, deploy code that writes to both and reads from the new structure, and backfill data in batches. Only after all instances run the new code do I contract by removing old columns in a later release. Migrations are versioned scripts in source control run by a tool such as Flyway or Alembic, executed as a controlled step before or after the rollout with locks and timeouts to prevent long blocking operations. I test migrations against a copy of production-sized data, and take a backup or snapshot. Destructive changes are separated from application releases so rollback of the app does not require rollback of data.
f: How do you avoid long locks?

q: How do you promote releases across environments using the same artifact and gates?
p: Build once, deploy the same digest to dev, staging and production with automated tests and approvals between stages.
tip: Promotion changes pointers, not binaries.
a: Promotion means moving a release candidate forward without rebuilding it. The pipeline builds once, pushes the image, and records its digest. Deploying to dev is automatic; promotion to staging happens after tests pass; and promotion to production requires gates such as smoke tests, vulnerability policy, change approval and sometimes a soak period. Technically promotion is updating a pointer: the image digest or version referenced by the environment's manifests in Git, or copying the same image to a production registry. Since the artifact is identical, results from staging are meaningful. I keep an audit record of which digest is in each environment and when. I also ensure each stage verifies the deployment with health checks, and that failures stop the promotion automatically. This is faster, safer and more traceable than rebuilding per environment.

q: A pipeline works on one runner but fails on another. How do you investigate?
p: Compare tool versions, environment variables, OS, permissions, network and caches; make the environment reproducible.
tip: Reproduce in the same image.
a: A difference between runners usually points to environment drift. I start by comparing the logs of a good and a bad run for tool versions, operating system, environment variables, installed packages, available disk and memory, and timestamps. Then I try to reproduce locally by running the same container image the job uses. Common causes are unpinned tool versions, an older cached dependency, different CPU architecture, missing network access or credentials on one runner pool, file permission or case-sensitivity differences, and leftover state on a long-lived runner. The permanent fix is to make the build hermetic: run jobs in a pinned container image, pin tool and dependency versions, use ephemeral runners and avoid relying on pre-installed software. I also add a step that prints key versions to the log so future differences are easy to spot.
f: What would you print for diagnostics?

q: A deployment is stuck in progress and pods never become ready. What do you check?
p: Describe the pods, check events, probes, image pulls, resource requests and config or secret mounts.
tip: Events first.
a: I begin with rollout status and then describe the pods, because events usually name the cause. Image pull errors show as ErrImagePull or ImagePullBackOff, pointing to a wrong tag, missing registry credentials or network issue. Pending pods suggest insufficient resources, unsatisfied node selectors, taints or an unbound volume. CrashLoopBackOff means the container starts and exits, so I read logs including the previous instance, and check configuration, missing environment variables or secrets, and database connectivity. If pods run but never become ready, the readiness probe is failing, perhaps due to the wrong path or port, a slow start needing a startup probe, or a dependency being down. I also check that the new ReplicaSet respects maxUnavailable and surge settings, and whether a quota or admission policy blocked creation. Once the cause is found I fix it in Git, not by editing live objects.
f: When do you use a startup probe?

q: Builds suddenly became slow after a dependency update. How do you diagnose?
p: Compare timing per step, check cache hits, dependency resolution and network, and bisect the change.
tip: Timing data per step first.
a: I start with data: compare step durations before and after the change in the pipeline's timing view. If dependency installation is slow, I check whether the cache key changed so the cache missed, whether a registry or proxy is slow or rate limiting, or whether the new dependency pulls a large transitive tree or compiles native code from source. If the build step is slower, a different compiler version or a new plugin may be the cause. I bisect by reverting the dependency bump or testing commits in between. Fixes can include restoring the cache, using a mirror, pinning versions, adding prebuilt binaries, parallelising or removing unneeded dependencies. Afterwards I add pipeline duration to a dashboard with an alert on regressions, so slowdowns are caught the same day. I review the setup regularly so it keeps matching how the team really works. I would also measure the effect, so the change is justified by data.
f: How do you tell a cache miss?
How do you bisect a slowdown?

q: A rollback did not fix the problem. What could explain that?
p: State outside the code changed: database migrations, configuration, feature flags, caches, dependencies or data.
tip: Rollback only reverts code.
a: If reverting the application did not resolve the issue, the cause probably lies in state or in something outside the deployed code. Possibilities include a database migration that is not backwards compatible or corrupt data written by the new version, a configuration or secret change applied separately, a feature flag turned on at the same time, a changed upstream dependency or third-party API, an expired certificate or credential, a cache or queue holding bad data, or an infrastructure change like a network rule. I compare the timeline of all changes around the start of the incident, not only deployments, using the change log and audit trails. Then I test hypotheses, for example disabling the flag or clearing the poisoned cache. This is why I try to make changes small, record every change in one timeline, and design migrations that tolerate rolling back the application.
f: What other changes do you check?
How do you make rollbacks safer?

q: Terraform apply in the pipeline failed halfway. How do you recover safely?
p: Do not rerun blindly: check state and lock, review what was created, then re-plan and apply the remainder.
tip: State is the source of truth, so protect it.
a: A partial failure leaves some resources created and recorded in state while others are missing. First I make sure nothing is still running and check the lock. If the lock is stale and I have verified the run is dead, I release it. Then I read the error: quota limits, permissions, dependency ordering and API throttling are typical. I review the state to see what exists, and run a plan, which should show only the remaining changes because Terraform tracks what succeeded. If a resource was created in the cloud but not recorded due to a crash, I import it instead of creating a duplicate. After fixing the cause, I apply again, preferably through the same pipeline so there is an audit trail. To reduce risk, I keep changes small, use remote state with locking and versioning, and avoid manual console changes.
f: What if a resource exists but is not in state?

q: Docker builds work locally but fail in CI with permission or network errors. What do you check?
p: Check runner user and permissions, registry credentials, proxy and DNS, build context size and rate limits.
tip: Look at auth and rate limits first.
a: Differences between my laptop and CI are usually about identity, network or context. For permission errors I check which user runs the build, whether the Docker socket or daemon is available, file ownership in the workspace and any read-only mounts. For network errors I check DNS, proxy settings, firewall or egress rules on the runner, and whether private registries and package indexes are reachable. Registry issues often come from missing or expired credentials, or from anonymous pull rate limits on public base images, which I solve by authenticating or mirroring base images in our own registry. I also compare the build context: a missing file due to dockerignore or a case-sensitive filesystem can break a build. Running the build with plain progress output and no cache reveals the failing step, and I reproduce it by running the same image locally.
f: How do you mirror base images?

q: ArgoCD shows an application as OutOfSync forever even after syncing. What is happening?
p: Usually a controller or webhook mutates fields, or defaults differ from the manifest. Configure ignore differences or fix the manifest.
tip: Read the diff.
a: If an application is perpetually OutOfSync, something keeps changing live fields so they differ from what Git declares. I run the app diff to see exactly which fields differ. Typical causes: a horizontal pod autoscaler or other controller changing replica counts, a mutating admission webhook or service mesh injecting sidecars and annotations, default values added by the API server that my manifest omits, a Helm chart rendering random values such as generated secrets or timestamps on each render, or a custom resource whose controller writes into the spec. Fixes depend on the cause: remove the field from the manifest if the controller owns it, configure ignore differences for that path, enable server-side apply, or make the template deterministic. I avoid ignoring broad areas because that can hide real drift. Cleaning noise is important so a real out-of-sync status keeps its meaning.
f: How do you read an app diff?

q: Intermittent pipeline failures show 'connection reset' or timeouts when downloading dependencies. What do you do?
p: Add a caching proxy or mirror, retries with backoff, pin versions and check runner network egress.
tip: Reduce dependence on the public internet.
a: Intermittent download failures usually come from the public registry being slow or rate limited, or from the runner's network or NAT having limits. I first check whether failures correlate with time, runner pool or specific hosts. The durable fix is to reduce reliance on the public internet: run an internal caching proxy or artifact repository that mirrors package registries and container base images, so builds fetch from a nearby, reliable source and still work when upstream is down. I also enable dependency caching keyed by lock files, configure sensible retries with exponential backoff, and set timeouts, instead of retrying whole pipelines manually. On the network side I check NAT gateway port exhaustion, DNS resolver performance and egress firewall rules. Monitoring pipeline failure reasons by category helps me see whether infrastructure flakiness is a trend and justify the fix.

q: A secret rotation broke deployments across many pipelines. How do you prevent a repeat?
p: Centralise secrets in a manager, reference them by name, rotate with overlap, and test rotation in staging.
tip: Dual validity during rotation.
a: The root issue is usually that the secret was copied into many places and each pipeline had its own stale value. I would centralise the secret in a manager and have pipelines reference it by name, so a rotation updates one source of truth. Rotation should support an overlap period where both old and new credentials are valid, so consumers can pick up the new one without a hard cutover. Better still, remove static secrets where possible by using short-lived credentials from workload identity. I inventory where each secret is used, announce rotations, and rehearse them in staging. After the incident, I add monitoring for authentication failures, an automated test that validates the credentials, and a runbook for rotation and rollback. This turns rotation from a risky event into a routine, low-impact operation.
f: Why overlap old and new credentials?
How do you find all users of a secret?

q: Design the approach to deploy 50 microservices with consistent pipelines but team autonomy.
p: Provide a golden-path template with reusable pipeline components, let teams extend it, and enforce guardrails centrally.
tip: Paved road, not forced road.
a: I would build a paved road: a versioned, reusable pipeline template maintained by a platform team that covers building, testing, scanning, signing, publishing and deploying, with sensible defaults. Teams call it with a few inputs, like language and service name, and can extend it with extra steps for their needs. Guardrails that matter, such as security scanning, artifact signing, and deployment gates for production, are enforced centrally through required workflows or admission policies, so they cannot be skipped. The platform versions the template, announces changes and supports an upgrade path with automated pull requests. Service teams own their services and their application-level tests. I would measure adoption and pipeline health, gather feedback regularly, and treat the platform as a product. This gives consistency, speed of onboarding and compliance without removing team ownership.
f: How do you roll out template changes?
